title: How Attackers Use AI as a Tool for Cyberattacks
content_md:
How Attackers Use AI as a Tool for Cyberattacks

A current report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) shows how the use of artificial intelligence by cybercriminals and state-sponsored groups has continued to evolve. Instead of sending individual commands to a chatbot, attackers are increasingly connecting language models with their own tools such as scanners, exploit frameworks, or shell access. This creates systems that can autonomously run through multiple steps of an attack, although humans still maintain control according to GTIG.

The AI Threat Tracker for Q3 2026 describes a shift: earlier attacks relied on isolated requests to an AI model. Now attackers link multiple tools together so that an AI system receives a target, develops an approach, executes actions, evaluates results, and adjusts its strategy as needed.

The reconnaissance phase of an attack is particularly well-suited to automation according to GTIG. An AI system can aggregate publicly accessible information, catalog domains and cloud resources, identify deployed software, and cross-reference with known vulnerabilities. Tasks that previously took analysts hours or days can be completed in less time.

A Q2 2026 example illustrates the pace of this development: a financially motivated attacker gained access to a cloud environment and deployed an AI-assisted coding assistant with prepared instructions. Within less than six hours, the group planned, built, and operated a large-scale credential harvesting campaign, compromising thousands of third-party credentials according to Google.

The system autonomously handled vulnerability scanning, troubleshooting during the attack, and IP rotation for obfuscation. Since the attack ran through the target company's own cloud infrastructure, the traffic appeared to external observers as regular, legitimate network traffic.

Google researchers also found an openly accessible control environment running an automated framework called Recon, containing instruction files for AI agents and storage for collected knowledge. Over 23,800 stolen credentials were organized and vetted through this system, including API keys for cloud and AI services. Google characterizes this as a shift from classic, passive malware toward actively directed, AI-supported credential harvesting.

GTIG also observes that AI systems can rapidly translate newly published vulnerabilities into concrete attack steps. In a separately documented campaign by a Chinese-speaking actor named knaithe, an agent called Hermes based on the DeepSeek model handled target search and vulnerability discovery. Through a pipeline called 1DayNews, vulnerability publications were collected, exploitability assessed, and suitable targets automatically forwarded.

Google emphasizes that no fully autonomous end-to-end attacks without human intervention against real targets have been observed so far. The documented direction is clear however: attackers are using AI support to gradually reduce manual effort across the entire attack chain.

Source: https://www.all-about-security.de/wie-angreifer-kuenstliche-intelligenz-als-werkzeug-fuer-cyberangriffe-einsetzen/
